edition.locus: Divine Institutes 6.9 (deum nosse colere / caput uirtutis / spes immortalitatis)

source_text: Huius legis caput primum est ipsum deum nosse, soli obtemperare, solum colere. non potest enim rationem hominis obtinere qui parentem animae suae deum nescit; quod est summum nefas. quae ignoratio facit ut diis aliis seruiat, quo nihil sceleratius committi potest. hinc iam procliuis est ad malitiam gradus per ignorantiam ueri ac singularis boni, quia deus, quem nosse refugit, fons est ipse bonitatis: uel si iustitiam sequi uolet, diuini tamen iuris ignarus gentis suae leges, tamquam uerum ius amplectetur, quas non utique iustitia, sed utilitas repperit. cur enim per omnes populos diuersa et uana iura sunt condita, nisi quod una quaeque gens id sibi sanxit quod putauit rebus suis utile? quantum autem ab iustitia recedat utilitas, populus ipse Romanus docet, qui per fetiales bella indicendo et legitime iniurias faciendo semperque aliena capiendo atque rapiendo possessionem sibi totius orbis comparauit. uerum hi iustos se putant, si contra leges suas nihil faciant: quod etiam timori adscribi potest, si praesentium poenarum metu sceleribus abstineant. sed concedamus sane ut id natura uel, ut ait philosophus, sua sponte faciant quod legibus facere coguntur. num idcirco iusti erunt, quia parent institutis hominum, qui ipsi aut errare aut iniusti esse potuerunt, sicut illi duodecim tabularum conditores, aut certe publicae utilitati pro condicione temporum seruierunt? aliut est igitur ciuile ius, quod pro moribus ubique uariatur, aliut uera iustitia, quam uniformem ac simplicem proposuit omnibus deus: quem qui ignorat, et ipsam iustitiam ignoret necesse est. sed putemus fieri posse ut aliquis naturali et ingenito bono ueras uirtutes capiat, qualem fuisse Cimonem Athenis accepimus, qui et egentibus stipem dedit et pauperes inuitauit et nudos induit, tamen cum illud unum quod est maximum deest, agnitio dei, iam bona illa omnia superuacua sunt et inania, ut frustra in iis adsequendis laborauerit. omnis enim iustitia eius similis erit humano corpori caput non habenti: in quo tametsi membra omnia et locis suis constent et figura et habitudine, tamen quoniam deest id quod est omnium principale, et uita et omni sensu caret. itaque membra illa formam tantummodo membrorum habent, usum non habent, tam scilicet quam caput sine corpore. cui similis est qui cum deum non ignoret, uiuit iniuste: id enim solum habet quod est summum, sed frustra, quoniam uirtutibus tamquam membris eget. itaque ut sit uiuum ac sensibile corpus, et agnitio dei necessaria est quasi caput et uirtutes omnes quasi corpus. ita fiet homo perfectus ac uiuus, sed tamen summa omnis in capite est, quod quamuis constare non possit sine omnibus, sine quibusdam tamen potest. et erit quidem animal uitiosum ac debile, sed tamen uiuet, sicut is qui et deum nouit et in aliqua re peccat; dat enim ueniam peccatis deus. itaque sine membris aliquibus uiui potest, sine capite nullo modo. haec res efficit ut philosophi etiamsi natura sint boni, tamen nihil sciant, nihil sapiant. omnis doctrina et uirtus eorum sine capite est, quia deum nesciunt, qui est uirtutis ac doctrinae caput. quem qui non adgnoscit, licet uideat, caecus est, licet audiat, surdus, licet loquatur, elinguis est. cum uero conditorem rerum parentemque cognouerit, tunc et uidebit et audiet et loquetur. habere enim caput coepit, in quo sunt sensus omnes conlocati hoc est oculi et aures et lingua. nam profecto is uidet qui ueritatem, in qua deus est, uel deum, in quo ueritas est, oculis cordis aspexerit, is audit qui diuinas uoces ac praecepta uitalia pectori suo adfigit, is loquitur qui caelestia disserens uirtutem ac maiestatem dei singularis enarrat. quare non est dubium quin impius sit quisquis deum non adgnouerit, omnesque uirtutes eius, quas habere aut tenere se putat., in illa mortifera uia reperiuntur, quae est tota tenebrarum. quapropter nihil est quod sibi aliquis gratuletur, si has inanes uirtutes adeptus est, quia non tantum miser, qui bonis praesentibus careat, sed etiam stultus sit necesse est, qui labores in uita sua maximos suscipiat in cassum. nam adempta spe immortalitatis quam deus pollicetur in sua religione uersantibus, cuius adsequendae gratia uirtus adpetenda est et quidquid malorum acciderit perferendum, maxima erit profecto uanitas obsequi uelle uirtutibus, quae frustra homini calamitates adferunt et labores. nam si uirtus est egestatem exilium dolorem mortem, quae timentur a ceteris, pati fortiter ac subire, quid tandem in se boni habet, cur eam philosophi propter se ipsam dicant expetendam ? nimirum superuacuis et inanibus poenis delectantur quibus licet agere tranquille. si enim mortales sunt auimae, si uirtus dissoluto corpore nihil futura est, quid fugimus adtributa nobis bona quasi aut ingrati aut indigni qui diuinis muneribus perfruamur? quae bona ut habeamus, scelerate inpieque uiuendum est, quia uirtutem id est iustitiam paupertas sequitur. sanus igitur non est qui nulla spe maiore proposita iis bonis quibus ceteri utuntur in uita, labores et cruciatus et miserias anteponat. si autem uirtus, ut ab ns rectissime dicitur, capessenda est, quia constet ad eam nasci hominem, subesse debet spes aliqua maior, quae malorum et laborum, quos perferre uirtutis est, magnum adferat praeclarumque solacium. nec aliter uirtus cum per se dura sit, haberi pro bono potest, quam si acerbitatem suam maximo bono penset. aeque non aliter his bonis praesentibus abstinendum est, quam si sint alia maiora, propter quae tanti sit et uoluptates omittere et mala omnia sustinere. ea uero nulla sunt alia, ut in tertio docui, nisi perpetuae uitae. hanc autem praestare quis potest nisi deus, qui uirtutem ipsam proposuit ? ergo in dei agnitione et cultu rerum summa uersatur: in hoc est spes omnis ac salus hominis, hic est sapientiae gradus primus, ut sciamus qui sit nobis uerus pater eumque solum pietate debita prosequamur, huic pareamus, huic deuotissime seruiamus, in eo promerendo actus omnis et cura et opera collocetur.
pass_a_gloss: The first head of this law is to know God, obey him alone, worship him alone. Not to know the Father of one's soul is the highest crime and slides into serving other gods. Even shining civic virtues without knowing God are empty — a body without a head. Whoever has not acknowledged God is impious; his virtues lie on the death-bearing dark road. Hope of immortality under God's religion makes virtue worth the pains; the sum is knowing and worshiping God.
pass_b_english: The first head of this law is to know God himself, to obey him alone, to worship him alone. For he cannot hold a human's reason who does not know God, the parent of his soul; which is the highest crime. Which ignorance makes him serve other gods, than which nothing more wicked can be committed. From here the step is already sloping toward malice through ignorance of the true and singular good, because God, whom he flees to know, is himself the fountain of goodness: or if he wills to follow justice, yet ignorant of divine right he will embrace his nation's laws as true right, which not justice but utility invented. For why have diverse and empty rights been founded through all peoples, except that each nation sanctioned for itself what it thought useful for its affairs? But how far utility withdraws from justice the Roman people itself teaches, which by declaring wars through the fetials and doing injuries legally and always taking and seizing others' things prepared for itself possession of the whole world. But these think themselves just if they do nothing against their own laws: which can also be ascribed to fear, if by dread of present punishments they abstain from crimes. But let us grant that by nature or, as the philosopher says, of their own accord they do what they are compelled by laws to do. Will they therefore be just because they obey humans' institutions, who themselves could either err or be unjust, as those founders of the Twelve Tables, or at least served public utility for the condition of the times? One thing therefore is civil right, which varies everywhere by manners, another true justice, which God has set uniform and simple for all: whom who does not know must necessarily also not know justice itself.

But let us suppose it can happen that someone by natural and inborn good takes true virtues, such as we have heard Cimon was at Athens, who both gave alms to the needy and invited the poor and clothed the naked: yet when that one thing which is greatest is missing, acknowledgment of God, already all those goods are superfluous and empty, so that he has labored in vain in pursuing them. For all his justice will be like a human body not having a head: in which although all the limbs both stand in their places and in shape and habit, yet because that which is principal of all is missing, it lacks both life and every sense. And so those limbs have only the form of limbs, they do not have use, as clearly as a head without a body. Like whom is he who though he does not not-know God lives unjustly: for he alone has what is highest, but in vain, since he lacks virtues as limbs. And so that there may be a living and sensible body, both acknowledgment of God is necessary as a head and all virtues as a body. So a human will become perfect and alive, but yet the whole sum is in the head, which although it cannot stand without all, still can without some. And he will indeed be a flawed and weak animal, but still will live, as he who both knows God and sins in some matter; for God gives pardon for sins. And so one can live without some limbs, without a head by no means. This fact makes it that philosophers, even if by nature they are good, still know nothing, are wise in nothing. All their teaching and virtue is without a head, because they do not know God, who is the head of virtue and teaching. Whom who has not acknowledged, though he may see, is blind, though he may hear, deaf, though he may speak, is tongueless. But when he has recognized the founder and parent of things, then he will both see and hear and speak. For he has begun to have a head, in which all the senses are placed, that is eyes and ears and tongue. For surely he sees who has looked with the heart's eyes on the truth, in which God is, or God, in whom truth is; he hears who fixes divine voices and life-giving precepts to his breast; he speaks who, discussing heavenly things, narrates the virtue and majesty of the singular God.

Wherefore there is no doubt that whoever has not acknowledged God is impious, and all his virtues, which he thinks he has or holds, are found on that death-bearing way, which is wholly of darkness. Therefore there is nothing for anyone to congratulate himself on if he has obtained these empty virtues, because not only must he be wretched who lacks present goods, but also foolish who takes up the greatest labors in his life in vain. For with the hope of immortality removed which God promises to those turning in his religion, for the sake of obtaining which virtue is to be sought and whatever evils happen are to be endured, there will certainly be the greatest emptiness in willing to obey virtues, which bring calamities and labors to a human in vain. For if virtue is to suffer and undergo bravely poverty, exile, pain, death, which are feared by the rest, what finally of good does it have in itself, why do the philosophers say it is to be sought for its own sake? Clearly they delight in superfluous and empty punishments, for whom it is allowed to live calmly. For if souls are mortal, if virtue after the body is dissolved will be nothing, why do we flee the goods assigned to us as if either ungrateful or unworthy to enjoy divine gifts? Which goods, that we may have them, one must live wickedly and impiously, because poverty follows virtue, that is justice. He is therefore not sound who with no greater hope set forward prefers labors and tortures and miseries to those goods which the rest use in life. But if virtue, as is most rightly said by us, is to be taken up, because it is agreed a human is born to it, some greater hope ought to underlie, which may bring great and splendid comfort of the evils and labors which it is virtue's to endure. And not otherwise can virtue, though hard in itself, be held for a good, than if it balances its bitterness with the greatest good. Equally not otherwise must one abstain from these present goods, than if there are other greater ones, for whose sake it is worth both omitting pleasures and sustaining all evils. But those are no others, as I taught in the third book, except of perpetual life. But who can furnish this except God, who has set virtue itself forward? Therefore the sum of things turns in acknowledgment and worship of God: in this is all hope and salvation of a human, this is the first step of wisdom, that we know who is our true father and follow him alone with due piety, obey him, serve him most devotedly, and that all act and care and work be placed in earning his favor.

lemmas.gloss: first law-head: know, obey, worship God alone
knowing God is the head; virtues are the body
sum of hope and salvation in knowing and worshiping God

choices.why: First head of the law is to know and worship God alone; utility is not justice.

rejected: alms and civic virtue suffice without God
choices.why: Virtues without knowing God are a headless body — form without life.

rejected: seek virtue for its own sake with mortal souls
choices.why: Immortality's hope under God's religion makes virtue's pains worth it; salvation is in his worship.
